title: Node.js vs the browser
idea: Node.js and the browser run the same JavaScript language, but each supplies different objects around it.

analogy.text: The same song played in a studio and on a stage. The notes are identical; the equipment around you is not.
analogy.breaks: Unlike notes, some built-in objects exist in both places, such as `fetch`.

points: The language is shared: syntax, `Array`, `Promise` and `Map` work in both.
The environment adds the rest: a browser adds the page, Node adds the machine.
Both environments also provide `console`, timers, `fetch` and `URL`.
Browsers sandbox a page; a Node script has the permissions of its user.

hero.title: Same language, different surroundings

left.title: Browser
items: Runs inside a web page, in a sandbox
Reads and changes the page through `document`
No free file access and no listening servers
Loads code with script tags or `import`

right.title: Node.js
items: Runs as a process on your computer
Reads files and listens for connections
Loads code with `require` or `import`; the modules page explains both

hero.verdict: The language is shared; the built-in objects are not.

code.title: What exists here?
code.caption: `typeof` is safe on names that may not exist. Run it here, then paste the same lines into a browser console and compare.

pitfalls: Do not use `document` or `window` in Node code; both throw a ReferenceError.
Guard shared code with `typeof window !== 'undefined'` before touching browser-only objects.
Read unfamiliar scripts before running them; Node gives them your full file and network access.

quiz.q: What does this print when run with `node`?
quiz.why: Node has no page, so `typeof window` is `undefined`. `process` is a Node object, so its type is `object`.

takeaway: Before you reuse code, check which built-in objects it touches.

starters: Can I reuse browser code in Node?
